title: True Orthophoto Generation from Aerial Frame Images and LiDAR Data: An Update
relevance: Names the defect that 197 prior papers in this tracker never mention: a conventional orthophoto is rectified with a bare-earth DTM, so ONLY THE BASE of a tree or building lands in its true position and everything above ground is displaced radially from nadir by an amount proportional to its height. This means our canopy polygons are systematically mislocated as a function of tree height and position within each photo frame, which contaminates the model-versus-reference comparison exactly along the height axis our staircase runs on - and it CONTRADICTS the implicit assumption behind every co-registration check we have done, none of which allowed for a height-dependent offset. It is also directly actionable: the method uses aerial frames plus LiDAR, and we already hold the Snohomish LiDAR.

title: Sub-meter tree height mapping of California using aerial images and LiDAR-informed U-Net model
relevance: Trains a U-Net regression on 60 cm NAIP RGB-NIR against an aerial-LiDAR canopy height model across an entire state, which is our proposed v045/v046 aux-height experiment already executed at scale and peer-reviewed, and it is the closest published precedent for the structural fix that iterations 68-69 narrowed us down to. It gives us an expected performance envelope before we spend Colab GPU time, and its report of robust reconstruction EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF IMAGE DISTORTION bears directly on whether relief displacement will defeat a height-aware model. NAIP 60 cm is also the exact source and resolution of our 2019n and 2022n acquisitions.

title: True orthophoto generation using multi-view aerial images
relevance: Documents the double-mapping and occlusion artefacts that conventional orthorectification produces in urban scenes, which matters to us because our 18 acquisitions were flown as different frame layouts, so each year carries a DIFFERENT displacement field. That predicts APPARENT CANOPY CHANGE WHERE NONE OCCURRED, concentrated on tall crowns and near buildings, and it is a threat to the pipeline's central deliverable - the 2000-2024 change series - rather than to any single-year accuracy number. If confirmed it would mean some measured canopy loss is a photogrammetric artefact, which no amount of extra labelling would fix.
